description: How a party label printed in a source (Party_As_Printed: a newspaper's or report's label, kept verbatim) is interpreted as a party or independent label on the site (Party_Name). The election manifest (scripts/build-test2-election-manifest.mjs, applyPartyLabelInterpretations) applies this file to every source contest: a rule fills Party_Name where it is blank and the printed label matches, unless it says override, when it also replaces the interpretation already there. Rules are tried in order and the first match wins, so a rule scoped to a body, a date window or named candidates is listed before a general one. Printed labels stay verbatim; only the interpretation changes. Variants of one party fold into the party's name on the site (U., Unionist, Official Unionist -> UUP); variants of one kind of independent fold into one (Ind., Indep., Inden. -> Independent); genuinely different organisations keep labels of their own. Honours and professions printed after a name (J.P., M.B.E., V.S.) are not party labels: the interpretation stays blank, which the site shows as 'No label', never as Independent. A ditto mark ('do.') takes the interpretation of the candidate printed above it. A printed label no rule settles keeps a blank interpretation; those are listed in the batch report with the evidence.

noLabel.reason: Honours and professions printed after a candidate's name (Justice of the Peace, M.B.E., O.B.E., V.S. = veterinary surgeon in the Downpatrick 1923 list beside J.P.), not party labels.

unresolved.where: Belfast aldermen, September 1946: Thomas Ferran (Falls, 714 votes against James Collins, Independent Labour) and Thomas Connor (Woodvale, 2,727 against Francis B. Loan, Unionist)
unresolved.searched: Irish Newspaper Archives, 2026-11-06: 'Ferran Falls', 'Connor Woodvale', '"workers candidate" Belfast' and 'Ferran Labour' (Belfast News-Letter), 1 August-15 October 1946. The News-Letter's nominations list (5 September 1946, p. 3) prints Connor as 'Workers' Candidate' and its results report (19 September 1946, p. 5) calls Ferran 'the "Workers' Candidate"'; neither names an organisation, and the Irish News has no 1946 issues in the archive. The Belfast Telegraph reports cited in the contests were not re-read.

ni.description: The Northern Ireland bodies, for rules marked "region": "ni": every county, borough, urban and rural district council and town commissioners of the six counties (the No. 2 rural districts are the County Armagh parts of the Castleblayney and Newry unions), the Northern Ireland Parliament, Assembly, Convention and Forum, the district councils of 1973 on (local-government), the Northern Ireland European Parliament constituency, the Northern Ireland referendums and the Ulster Unionist Party's internal leadership contests (uup-leadership). Every body folder under data/elections-source/data/elections is in this list or in notNi; tests/elections/party-label-regions.test.mjs fails when one is added to neither.

notNi.description: Outside Northern Ireland: the Dail and the Republic's local, European and presidential elections and referendums, the Mayor of Limerick and the Seanad, where a bare 'Labour' is the Irish Labour Party, with Fianna Fáil's internal leadership and presidential-nomination ballots; and the House of Commons, whose Irish seats before 1922 are not Northern Ireland seats (Dublin College Green 1915 'Labour' is Irish Labour).

rules.evidence: Warrenpoint 1952 West Ward: the paper prints no party beyond 'Lab.'; the label is inferred from the 1955 and 1958 prints, where the same Labour men (McGreevy, Barry, Hughes) stand as Irish Labour (I.L.), as Fay and McMullan already are in 1952 (research-J W8R-4, owner-approved 13 Nov 2026).

Warrenpoint 1936 (Fay, O'Hagan) and 1946 (the West Ward slate and Rice in the East Ward), printed 'Lab.': a town Labour list with no organisation named, the nationalist Labour men who stood as Irish Labour from 1952; not the Northern Ireland Labour Party. Read as Labour with no party named ('Local Labour'), as Warrenpoint 1923 is (research-J W8R-4, owner-approved 13 Nov 2026).
Warrenpoint 1926: J.P. is an honour; (U.) is the Unionist label.
Warrenpoint 1929: J.P. is an honour; (I.) is the Independent label.
Warrenpoint 1929: printed as a Unionist who was also on the town's Progressive list; U. is the party label.

Newry 1964 was a split in the Irish Labour group that held all twelve nationalist seats in 1961: the South Ward note reads 'Irish Labour panel took all six seats' (Newry Reporter, 28 May 1964, p. 6). I.L. there is Irish Labour, not Independent Labour.
Newry 1964: the West Ward note reads 'Newry Labour swept all six seats' (Newry Reporter, 28 May 1964, p. 6), the breakaway from the Irish Labour panel (I.L.).

Warrenpoint 1929: the National League of the North, Joseph Devlin's Nationalist organisation founded in May 1928, which the site files as the Nationalist Party (as it files 'National League' in Newry No. 2).

Derry 1949: the Irish Labour Party, which the Derry Labour group (Stephen McGonagle among its candidates) joined in 1949 after the NILP declared for the Union (Wikipedia, Stephen McGonagle). Not the British Independent Labour Party.

Derry South Ward 1946: the joint list printed by the Derry Journal (18 Oct 1946, p. 5); Wikipedia's 1946 Londonderry Borough Council election files W. Barr, James Deeney and W. Mullan as Derry Labour Party, an anti-partition left-wing party separate from the NILP.
Derry South Ward 1946: Wikipedia's 1946 Londonderry Borough Council election files T. Doherty, Daniel Barr and P. J. Downey as Nationalist / Anti-Partition; all three stood as A.P. in 1949.

Bare 'Labour' in Northern Ireland (batch 4b). A source reading of plain 'Labour' was turned into Irish Labour by normalizeParty, a Dail convention, so about 90 Northern Ireland council candidacies showed as Irish Labour; the rules below read each by its place and date, and only in the ni region, so no Dail or Republic contest changes. Where the paper printed Irish Labour, Eire Labour or E.L., the reading is Irish Labour: Patrick Agnew, Armagh County Council 1949, printed 'Irish Labour' (Newry Reporter, 9 June 1949, p. 3; he had joined the Irish Labour Party that year).

Armagh North-West Ward 1961 and 1964: Thomas Reilly was nominated as 'Labour' and described in the result as an Independent Trade Unionist (Armagh Guardian, 18 May 1961, p. 4; Belfast Telegraph, 21 May 1964, p. 4, 'Independent T.U.'): an independent of the Labour kind, not a party nominee.

Belfast 1920 (Pottinger, Victoria, Woodvale): nominees of the National Amalgamated Union of Labour, printed N.A.U.L. beside the Belfast Labour Party's B.L.P. on the same results sheets (PR Society of Ireland, Report and Analysis of the P.R. Urban Elections in Ulster, 1920), so not the Belfast Labour Party; Wikipedia's 1920 Belfast Corporation election files them as NAUL, apart from Belfast Labour. S. Bradley stood as an official Unionist in Woodvale in 1923.

Camlough 1952: no label printed; at the count James Maginnis said 'the Labour Party would return to the fight' (Newry Reporter, 12 June 1952, p. 8). In 1952 the Labour Party of the Newry district was the Irish Labour Party: the NILP had expelled members of the Irish Labour Party and the Anti-Partition League in May 1949 (Strabane Chronicle, 21 May 1949, p. 1), South Armagh's Labour member Patrick Agnew stood as Irish Labour in 1949, and Newry's Labour list stood as E.L. (Eire Labour) in 1955 and Irish Labour in 1961, as Ballybot in Newry No. 2 did in 1958.

Lurgan 1949 (R. Levin, M. Casey, H. Haughey, V. McKenna, printed L): 'four members of a local Labour group' (Belfast News-Letter, 17 June 1949, p. 4; Irish News, 17 June 1949, p. 2), 'the local Labour group ... all Catholics' (Irish News, 16 June 1949, p. 3). No party is named, and in June 1949 the group was no longer of the NILP, which had just barred anti-partitionists.

Belfast January 1923 (Lab.: Gordon, Scott, Malcolm, Milan, Kyle, Donaldson): 'NO OFFICIAL LABOUR MEN. The local Labour Party are not putting forward any candidates officially', the men nominated being 'prominently identified with the Labour movement' (Belfast News-Letter, 6 January 1923, p. 5). Batch 4 read them as the Belfast Labour Party; the party did not nominate them, so they are read as Labour with no party named.

Before the Northern Ireland Labour Party was formed (March 1924, from the Belfast Labour Party): Lurgan 1899-1920 ('working-men's (Labour) candidates', Lurgan Mail, 20 January 1900), Portadown, Lisburn and Tandragee 1920, Strabane 1920 and January 1923, Ballymena and Dromore 1923, Warrenpoint 1923 (seven 'Labour (anti-Partitionist)' men, contest note). Town Labour lists with no organisation named in the sources; outside Belfast there was no Belfast Labour Party to read them as, and the Irish Labour Party is not named. Read as Labour with no party named ('Local Labour'), never as Irish Labour.

From the NILP's foundation in March 1924, a bare Labour in a Northern Ireland contest is the Northern Ireland Labour Party unless the paper printed Irish Labour (rule above) or the context shows another body (rules above): Armagh County Council 1939 (Patrick Agnew, NILP member for South Armagh at Stormont 1938-45; F. J. Morris), Newry No. 2 1939, Keady 1939, Armagh 1946 ('Official Lab.' against Independent Labour), Lurgan 1946 ('Labour Party') and 1967, Portadown 1967 (L, as the NILP's L. of 1955-61), Strabane 1939-67. Strabane's Labour councillors (1939-67) are the weakest of these: no source read names their party, so the default applies.
Belfast 1923 (Falls, Smithfield): the contest note reads 'E.W. = Expelled Workers' nominees (News-Letter, 6 January 1923)', the Catholic workers expelled from the shipyards in 1920.

Belfast 1938: the Northern Ireland Individual Traders and Anti-Monopolist Association, which nominated in eight wards (contest notes, Belfast News-Letter 9 and 17 May 1938). 'Ind.' is Individual, not Independent.
Belfast 1949 (Falls, Smithfield): the contest note reads 'The News-Letter labels the three unsuccessful candidates Nationalist (Nat.); the Irish News calls them Inter-Party.'

Dungannon West Ward 1964: Patricia McCluskey and her running mates, the Campaign for Social Justice founded in Dungannon in January 1964 (Wikipedia, Patricia McCluskey; she was one of four CSJ members elected in May 1964).
Bangor 1964-67, Downpatrick 1967, Ballycastle 1967: the Ulster Liberal Party (1956-87), the only Liberal organisation contesting Northern Ireland elections then.
Ballycastle and Downpatrick 1967: the National Democratic Party (1965-70), as the site already files N.D.P. in Belfast and NDP in Strabane.
Derry 1938-52, Enniskillen 1955: anti-partition nominees (from 1945 the Anti-Partition League), filed under the site's existing Anti-Partitionist label as AP is in Newry No. 2.
Banbridge 1949: the official Labour (NILP) candidates, as against independent Labour; the NILP is the Labour party organised in County Down in 1949.
Omagh 1961: the Nationalist Party's own nominees, as 'Official N' is filed in County Armagh.
Downpatrick 1964 (two candidates beside a Nationalist list), as Nat. Lab. is filed in Keady.
Belfast 1949, Warrenpoint 1961: the Irish Labour Party, as Eire Lab. and Irish Lab. are filed.
Belfast 1952: an unofficial (not endorsed) Irish Labour candidate, an independent of the Labour kind, as 'unofficial Unionist' is filed Independent Unionist.
Variants of Independent; non-party is filed Independent in Lurgan.
Variants of Independent Unionist; an unofficial Unionist is filed Independent Unionist.
Derry 1928: H. N. Greenway, passed over by the Unionist ward committee, stood as an Independent Labour Unionist (contest note, Derry Journal 6, 9 and 18 January 1928): an independent Unionist.
Variant of Independent Nationalist.
Variant of Independent Labour.

Belfast 1925-31: the Belfast News-Letter's name for the Northern Ireland Labour Party's candidates, not a separate party. The Irish News reports the same 1925 results as 'in Smithfield the Labour candidate, Mr. Wm. M'Mullan; in Dock the Labour candidate, Mr. Harry Midgley' (16 January 1925, p. 7) where the News-Letter headed them 'two Socialist gains' (16 January 1925, p. 7), and in 1928 calls Sam Kyle, printed Soc. in Duncairn, 'the Labour leader' (Irish News, 17 January 1928, p. 4). The candidates are the NILP's: Midgley, Kyle, McMullan (NILP MP for Belfast West 1925), Clarke Scott, Dawson Gordon, Robert Getgood, Margaret McCoubrey; the same men are printed Lab. (read NI Labour) in 1924, 1926 and 1931-32. Batch 4 read them as 'Socialist', sharing that party page with a 1999-2014 Republic label; they now count with NI Labour and the Socialist page is the Republic label's alone.
The town ratepayers' associations (Bangor 1928-67, Coleraine 1929, Cookstown 1946, Newtownabbey 1967), filed under one label as R.A. already is in Armagh.
Coleraine 1929, Kilkeel 1946: printed as the British Legion's candidates.

Limavady 1946 (J. L. Ritter, 'Ex-Servicemen') and Portadown 1952 (H. McCourt, 'Ex-Ser.', described only as 'an ex-serviceman'): ex-servicemen's candidates whose sources do not name the British Legion, so they have a label of their own; only a label printed as the Legion's is read as British Legion (batch 4b).

Newry 1946, 1949, 1955 and 1958: the Irish Citizen Association (the 1958 contest note itself gives the new council as 'Labour 9, Unionist 6, Irish Citizen Association 3'). The Irish Press lists the 1946 nominees as 'Irish Citizen Association candidates' by ward (Keogh, McMahon, Bennett, Casey and Malone in the South Ward; Connellan, Larkin, Hunter and others in the West) (Irish Press, 6 September 1946, p. 5; the association's teams are forecast in the Irish Press, 24 August 1946, p. 10). In 1955 the Irish News reports 'a sweeping victory for the Irish Citizen Association', which held ten seats before the poll and eleven after, under the heading 'I.C.A.'s sweeping victory over Labour at Newry' (Irish News, 20 May 1955, p. 3; Irish Newspaper Archives page INW19550520.1.3). Not Lurgan's Independent Citizens' Association of 1964-67.

Belfast Clifton 1923: James Hanvey, leather merchant, 'who stood as an Independent Unionist' (Belfast News-Letter, 16 January 1923, p. 5); he was not on the official Unionist list (News-Letter, 8 January 1923, p. 5).

Belfast Woodvale 1923: William Addis, an engineers' candidate (the Irish News prints 'Engineer'), is one of the 'Labour members of the present Corporation seeking re-election' with Dawson Gordon and Clarke Scott, in a year when the Labour Party nominated no one officially (Belfast News-Letter, 6 January 1923, p. 5): read as the other Labour men of 1923 are.
Belfast 1924, as TTA and 'Tenants' Association nominee' are filed.
Belfast Court Ward 1933 and 1936: unemployed workers' candidates, a label of their own.
Belfast Duncairn 1936: William Bradbury, elected for the Jubilee Protestant Defence Association against an official Unionist.
Newry South Ward 1929-39: W. F. Cunningham, printed T.U. (1929), Trade Unionist Labour (1932) and Trades Union Labour (1939), standing apart from the Labour list in each year.
Portadown 1952: 'Trades C. Mid-Ulster Trades Council' (contest note); T. Newell became the first Mid-Ulster Trades Council representative on the council.

Local Progressive lists: Warrenpoint 1926 and 1936 (the 1936 contest turned on mixed bathing), Carrickfergus 1938 (against the Efficiency Party), Ballyclare 1946. Not the Progressive Unionists of 1938 or the PUP.
Carrickfergus 1938: a local ticket of its own, against the Progressives.
Holywood 1927: printed Conservative, kept as Conservative.
One party: the site files the Northern Ireland Labour Party as NI Labour before 1973; the County Armagh pilot used the full name.

Dáil general election 2016 (owner's decision, 13 November 2026): the Independent Alliance was a grouping of independents, not a registered party; its 21 candidates stood as non-party candidates (the official returns give each as Non-Party, NON-P.), so they are shown as Independent, as on the ballot paper. ElectionsIreland labels them Independent Alliance and Wikipedia's count tables Independent Alliance (Ireland); each contest's source note (source-checked-fixes batch independent-alliance-2016-2026-11-13) names the members of the grouping. The South Kerry Independent Alliance and other bodies and years are not matched.
